candidates.background: Orlando Sanchez was born in Cuba, is an Air Force veteran, and attended Bellaire High School and the University of Houston. He served on the Houston City Council from 1995 to 2001 and as Harris County Treasurer from 2007 to 2018, and ran unsuccessfully for Houston mayor in 2001 and 2003 and for city controller in 2019 and 2023. priorities.text: Calls fiscal responsibility the most important part of his campaign and says he would rein in county spending and scrub the budget.
Lists cutting property taxes, creating a regional public safety district, and using voter-approved flood bond money as top priorities.
Campaigns on election integrity, streamlined county operations, tighter travel spending, and eliminating what he calls "left-wing employment practices."
Says the county should expand its courts and jail and expand access to health care, particularly for people with mental illness.

promises.text: Says he would lower the county property tax rate in his first budget, without specifying by how much.
Pledged at an October 2026 forum to support raising $1 million for at least three new community lighthouse resilience hubs and $500,000 for the Capital IDEA Houston workforce program.
Pledged to seek future flood control bond elections once 2018 bond funds are spent.

record.text: As county treasurer, made efficiencies that returned funds to the general fund, according to the Chronicle.
Says he voted for property tax cuts as a member of the Houston City Council.

notes.text: Won the March 2026 Republican primary with 26.5 percent and the May runoff with 63.3 percent over Warren Howell.

The Chronicle editorial board endorsed his opponent in the general election, rating Sanchez 3 of 5 stars, and noted he said he would vote for Railroad Commission nominee Bo French and later declined to say whether he still backed French after French's racist social media posts.
A University of Houston Hobby School survey released October 13, 2026 showed Sanchez at 40 percent to 47 percent for Plummer among likely voters.
In the Houston Bar Association's 2026 poll (not an endorsement), Sanchez received 282 votes to 271 for Letitia Plummer.

q_county_tax.summary: Says county taxes are too high and he would lower the property tax rate in his first budget, opposing the 2026 county tax increase.

q_county_mental.summary: Calls for treatment for people with serious mental health needs who end up in the county jail and for expanded health care access for people with mental illness.

issue_notes.summary: calls flooding a regional problem requiring cooperation with neighboring counties, and proposes accelerating the Kingwood Diversion Channel and Taylor Gully projects and joining the Lake Houston dredging district.
proposes agreements letting the nearest available law enforcement unit respond to emergencies across jurisdictional lines.

candidates.current_role: Dentist; former Houston City Council member, At-Large Position 4 (2020 to 2025)
candidates.background: Letitia Plummer is a dentist and small business owner who served on the Houston City Council in At-Large Position 4 from 2020 through 2025. She ran unsuccessfully for Congress in 2018. She won the 2026 Democratic nomination for county judge by defeating former Houston Mayor Annise Parker in a May runoff.

priorities.text: Says it is time for the county to "tighten the belt" and examine where it spends the most money, while seeking more state and federal infrastructure funding.

Names justice (including expanding Cite and Release and non-police emergency response), a county housing trust fund, and funding Harris Health clinics and behavioral health services as top priorities.
Calls disaster resilience her primary priority, including neighborhood resilience hubs that can operate off the grid.
Wants to continue county services beyond infrastructure and public safety, including mental health, financial literacy, and small business support.

promises.text: Says she would not renew or would cancel the county's Flock license plate camera contract as written and would require published use policies, audits, and data limits.
Pledged at an October 2026 forum to support raising $1 million for at least three new community lighthouse resilience hubs and full funding for Harris Health.
Pledged to seek future flood control bond elections once 2018 bond funds are spent.
Says she would create a dedicated County Housing Trust Fund and offer down payment assistance for first-time homebuyers.

record.text: On the Houston City Council, pushed a police reform proposal, tenant protections for substandard apartments, and limits on Houston Police Department cooperation with federal immigration agents.
Says she secured funding for the first generator at the Kashmere Gardens Multipurpose Center while on the council.

notes.text: Finished second in the March 2026 Democratic primary with 37.3 percent and won the May runoff with 51.1 percent over Annise Parker.

The Chronicle editorial board endorsed her (3.5 of 5 stars), and noted she has filed faulty campaign finance reports and was sanctioned twice by the Texas State Board of Dental Examiners, most recently in 2022.
A University of Houston Hobby School survey released October 13, 2026 showed Plummer at 47 percent to 40 percent for Sanchez among likely voters.
In the Houston Bar Association's 2026 poll (not an endorsement), Plummer received 271 votes to 282 for Orlando Sanchez.

q_county_tax.summary: Opposed the 2026 county property tax increase and supports finding efficiencies, but declined to commit to lowering the rate and said she would not cut county programs.

q_county_mental.summary: Lists expanding behavioral health services and non-police emergency response among her top priorities and wants the county to keep funding mental health services.

issue_notes.summary: supports building a new, fully staffed and more humane jail rather than a larger one, while reducing the jail population and speeding case processing.
proposes bringing in more small and midsize contractors, paying them promptly, and planning better around state and federal funding rules.
wrote that the county should comply with the letter of the law on immigration enforcement and not go beyond its requirements.
criticized using temporary COVID-era federal funds for permanent programs and says residents should have been told when programs relied on temporary funding.
